deep.reconstruction:
This page sits in the 1983 'Théories homotopiques' notes, the period of Pursuing Stacks, and anticipates Les Dérivateurs. (The neighbouring 'pages' are unrelated administrative forms.)

Setting. M is a category with a class of weak equivalences W. For each small index category A, H_W(A) is the localization of the functor category M^A (or Hom(A,M)) at the pointwise weak equivalences. A ↦ H_W(A) is the prederivator of (M,W). For a functor f: A→B of index categories there is a restriction f^H = f^*: H_W(B) → H_W(A).

Opening sentence. Grothendieck says he is interested in the cases where every f^H has a left adjoint f^H_! and a right adjoint f^H_*. These are homotopy left and right Kan extensions, i.e. homotopy colimits and limits relative to a base. He expects this to hold under suitable conditions on W. This is essentially the derivator axiom on existence of Kan extensions.

Remark. Let f: M → M' be a functor with f(W) ⊂ W'. It induces functors H_W(A) → H_{W'}(A). These are (bi)functorial in A, i.e. pseudo-natural, and compatible with the restriction functors u^*. So f gives a morphism of prederivators.

This does not a priori mean that the morphism commutes with the Kan extension operations u_!, u_*. Commutation is only up to a canonical base-change (mate) map, which need not be invertible.

Example. If W and W' consist only of isomorphisms, then H_W(A) = M^A. Commutation with u_! (resp. u_*) then means exactly that f preserves the relevant colimits (resp. limits), i.e. f commutes with lim→ (resp. lim←).

Last line. 'But of course' if H_W(A) → H_{W'}(A) is an equivalence for all A, commutation holds automatically: an equivalence preserves adjoints, so the mates are isomorphisms.

Modern statement: a morphism of derivators need not be cocontinuous or continuous; an equivalence of derivators always is.
errors: The letter f is used both for functors between index categories (f^H, f_!, f_*) and for the functor M → M'. This is a notational clash rather than a mathematical error.
Commutation should be understood via the canonical mate/base-change 2-cell; the page leaves this implicit.
The final sentence is cut off, so the conclusion about equivalences is only stated, not argued. It is nevertheless correct: equivalences transport adjoints.

ideas.what: Prederivator A ↦ W^{-1}(M^A) attached to a category with weak equivalences, with restriction functors and their adjoints f_!, f_* (homotopy Kan extensions) under conditions on W
ideas.modern_name: (pre)derivator of a homotopy theory; homotopy Kan extensions
ideas.usually_credited_to: Grothendieck (Les Dérivateurs, ~1990); independently Heller (Homotopy theories, 1988); Franke (systems of triangulated diagram categories)

ideas.what: A weak-equivalence-preserving functor M→M' induces a morphism of prederivators compatible with u^*, but not necessarily with u_!, u_*. In the trivial-W case this reduces to preservation of colimits/limits. An equivalence automatically commutes.
ideas.modern_name: cocontinuous/continuous morphisms of derivators; mates / Beck–Chevalley
ideas.usually_credited_to: Grothendieck (Les Dérivateurs); later systematized by Maltsiniotis, Groth, Cisinski
ideas.where_published: Les Dérivateurs (morphismes de dérivateurs commutant aux images directes homologiques/cohomologiques)

deep.surprise_reason: These are standard foundational remarks on derivators, already present in Pursuing Stacks and Les Dérivateurs. The only point of mild interest is the early (1983) date of the formulation.
transcription_corrections: Line 1–3: read 'On s'intéresse aux cas où les f^H ont des adjoints à g[auche] f^H_! et à droite f^H_*, sous conditions sur W.' The transcription's 'et des adjoints' should be 'ont des adjoints'.
'(compatible[?] avec f^*_W, f^*_{W'})' is plausible, meaning compatibility with the restriction functors.
'qu'il "commute" à des paires aux[?] f_!, f_*' should probably read 'qu'il "commute" aux opérations f_!, f_*' or similar.
'si W, W' sont identités aux iso' should read 'si W, W' sont réduits aux iso'.
'cette commutation [-signe-] signifie pour f_! (resp. f_*) que f commute aux lim→ (resp. lim←)'. The insertion '(Coeq (?))' is likely '(resp. f_*)', and 'ses f' is likely 'que f'.
In the last line, 'A^?' is most likely just A.
